“Conclusive of what?”
“My dear fellow, can you really fail to see how directly it concerns the case?”
“I cannot say I see it—unless he wanted to deny the signature if she sued him for breaking his promise to marry.”

“No, that is not it. Still, two letters should settle everything. I shall send one to a firm in the City and the other to her stepfather, Mr. Windibank, asking him to meet us here tomorrow evening at six. It is as well to conduct our business with the male relatives. Until replies arrive, Doctor, there is nothing more to do. We can put this little problem aside for the time being.”

I had seen so many proofs of my friend's subtle reasoning and extraordinary energy in action that I felt sure his calm confidence rested on solid grounds. He could not be treating this strange mystery so easily without good reason. I had known him fail only once, over the King of Bohemia and Irene Adler's photograph. When I remembered the uncanny affair of the Sign of Four and the extraordinary events of the Study in Scarlet, I felt that a puzzle would have to be very tangled indeed to defeat him.

I left him then, still puffing away at his black clay pipe, convinced that when I returned the following evening I would find him in possession of all the clues needed to establish the identity of Miss Mary Sutherland's disappearing bridegroom.

A seriously ill patient was occupying my own attention at the time, and I spent the entire following day at the sufferer's bedside. I was not free until nearly six, when I jumped into a hansom and drove to Baker Street, rather afraid of arriving too late to witness the little mystery's _dénouement_. But Holmes was alone, half asleep, his long, thin body curled into the depths of his armchair. A formidable collection of bottles and test-tubes, together with the sharp, clean smell of hydrochloric acid, showed that he had spent the day on his beloved chemical experiments.
“Well, have you found the answer?” I asked on entering.
“Yes. It proved to be bisulphate of baryta.”
“No, no—the mystery!” I exclaimed.

“Oh, that! I was thinking of the salt I have been examining. There was never any mystery about this affair, although, as I said yesterday, some details are interesting. The only difficulty is that I fear no law can reach the scoundrel responsible.”
“Then who was he, and why did he abandon Miss Sutherland?”
I had scarcely finished speaking, and Holmes had not yet opened his mouth to answer, when we heard a heavy footstep in the passage and a knock at the door.
“That will be the young lady's stepfather, Mr. James Windibank,” Holmes said. “He wrote to say he would arrive at six. Come in!”

The newcomer was a stocky man of medium height, about thirty, clean-shaven and sallow, with a smooth, ingratiating manner. His grey eyes were extraordinarily sharp and penetrating. He looked enquiringly from one of us to the other, placed his glossy top-hat on the sideboard, and, with a small bow, edged into the nearest chair.
“Good evening, Mr. James Windibank,” Holmes said. “I believe you sent this typed letter arranging to see me at six?”

“Yes, sir. I am afraid I am slightly late, but my time is not entirely my own. I regret that Miss Sutherland has troubled you with this little business. Such dirty linen is much better kept out of public view. I strongly opposed her coming, but, as you may have noticed, she is excitable and impulsive, and difficult to manage once she has made up her mind. Naturally, I objected less to you, since you have no official connection with the police. Still, nobody wants a family misfortune of this kind broadcast abroad. Besides, it is money wasted. How could you possibly find this Hosmer Angel?”
“On the contrary,” Holmes replied quietly, “I have every reason to expect that I shall succeed in finding Mr. Hosmer Angel.”
Windibank gave a violent start and let his gloves fall. “I am delighted to hear that,” he said.

“It is curious,” Holmes observed, “how individual a typewriter can be—quite as distinctive as someone's handwriting. Unless they are brand new, no two machines produce exactly the same result. Some letters wear more than others, and some wear on one side only. In this note of yours, Mr. Windibank, you will notice that the ‘e’ is slightly blurred throughout, while the tail of the ‘r’ has a small defect. There are fourteen further characteristics, but those are the easiest to see.”
“That machine handles all our office correspondence, so it is probably rather worn,” our visitor replied, watching Holmes closely with his bright little eyes.

“Now let me show you something genuinely interesting, Mr. Windibank,” Holmes continued. “One of these days I mean to write another short monograph, this time on the typewriter's connection with crime. I have given the subject some attention. Here are four letters supposedly written by the missing gentleman. Every one is typed. In each, you find not only blurred ‘e’s and ‘r’s without tails, but also, if you care to examine them through my magnifying glass, all fourteen of the other characteristics I mentioned.”
Windibank sprang up and seized his hat. “I cannot waste my time on this fanciful nonsense, Mr. Holmes. If you can catch the man, do so, and let me know when you have.”
“Certainly,” Holmes replied, walking to the door and locking it. “Then let me inform you that I have caught him!”
“What! Where?” Mr. Windibank shouted, turning white to the lips and looking around him like a rat caught in a trap.

“Oh, that will not do—not at all,” Holmes said smoothly. “There is no escape from this, Mr. Windibank. It is entirely transparent. You paid me a poor compliment in suggesting that I could not solve such a simple problem. There! Sit down, and we can discuss it.”
Our visitor sank into a chair, his face deathly pale, sweat gleaming on his forehead. “It—it isn't grounds for legal action,” he stammered.

“I very much fear you are right. But between ourselves, Windibank, in its petty way this is as cruel, selfish, and heartless a trick as I have ever encountered. Let me go through what happened, and correct me wherever I am wrong.”

The man huddled in his chair, his head bowed to his chest, looking utterly defeated. Holmes rested his feet on a corner of the mantelpiece and leaned back, hands in pockets. He began to speak, seemingly more to himself than to us.

“A man married a much older woman for her money,” he began. “While her daughter lived with them, he also enjoyed the daughter's income. For people in their circumstances it was a substantial sum; losing it would make a serious difference. Keeping it was worth some effort. The daughter was good-natured and agreeable, but also loving and warm-hearted. With her decent looks and small income, she plainly would not remain unmarried for long. Her marriage would mean losing a hundred pounds a year. How, then, could her stepfather prevent it? First he did the obvious: kept her at home and forbade her to mix with people her own age. Soon, though, he saw that this would not work indefinitely. She became restless, asserted her rights, and finally declared that she would attend a particular ball. What did her clever stepfather do next? He devised a plan that spoke better for his ingenuity than for his heart. With his wife's knowledge and assistance, he disguised himself: tinted spectacles hid those sharp eyes, a moustache and thick side-whiskers concealed his face, and that clear voice became a persuasive whisper. Her short sight made him doubly safe. He appeared as Mr. Hosmer Angel and excluded rival suitors by courting her himself.”
“It began as a joke,” our visitor groaned. “We never imagined she would take it so much to heart.”

“Very possibly not. Whatever your intention, she certainly did take it to heart. Convinced that her stepfather was in France, she never for a moment suspected any deception. His attentions flattered her, and her mother's loudly expressed approval strengthened their effect. Then Mr. Angel began visiting the house: clearly the affair had to be carried as far as possible to make it effective. Meetings followed, then an engagement, which would prevent her affections from wandering towards anyone else. But the deception could not last forever. Pretending to travel to France was becoming awkward. The obvious solution was to end the affair so dramatically that it left a lasting mark on her mind and kept her from considering another suitor for a long time. Hence the vows of loyalty sworn on a Testament; hence the hints that something might happen on the very morning of the wedding. James Windibank wanted Miss Sutherland so devoted to Hosmer Angel, and so uncertain of his fate, that she would refuse to listen to another man for at least ten years. He brought her to the church door. Unable to go any further, he conveniently disappeared, using the old trick of entering one door of a four-wheeler and leaving through the other. That, I believe, is the sequence of events, Mr. Windibank!”
During Holmes's account our visitor had regained some of his confidence. He now stood, a cold sneer spreading across his pale face.

“Perhaps so, Mr. Holmes, perhaps not,” he said. “But if you are as clever as you think, you should know that you are the one breaking the law now. Nothing I have done from the outset gives grounds for action. Keeping that door locked, however, makes you liable for assault and unlawful restraint.”

“As you say, the law cannot touch you,” Holmes replied, unlocking the door and flinging it open. “Yet no man ever deserved punishment more. If the young lady has a brother or a friend, he ought to take a whip to your shoulders. By Jove!” he continued, reddening at the man's malicious sneer. “This is no part of my duty to my client, but there is a hunting crop within reach, and I think I shall allow myself the pleasure of—” He took two quick strides towards it. Before he could grasp it, however, footsteps clattered wildly down the stairs and the heavy front door slammed. From the window we could see Mr. James Windibank racing down the street.

“What a cold-blooded villain!” Holmes said with a laugh, dropping back into his chair. “He will go from one crime to another until he does something dreadful and finishes on the gallows. In some respects, the case has not been altogether uninteresting.”
“Even now, I cannot follow every step in your reasoning,” I remarked.

“From the beginning, of course, it was plain that Mr. Hosmer Angel must have had a powerful reason for behaving so strangely. It was equally clear that the stepfather was the only man who, as far as we could see, actually benefited from this affair. The fact that they never appeared together was suggestive: one always came on the scene when the other was away. The tinted spectacles and peculiar voice hinted at a disguise, as did the thick whiskers. His curious decision to type his signature confirmed all my suspicions. That implied his handwriting was so familiar to her that she would recognise even the tiniest specimen. You see, these separate facts, together with many smaller ones, all pointed in the same direction.”
“How did you confirm those suspicions?”

“Once I had identified my man, confirmation was easy. I knew which firm employed him. I took the printed description and removed everything a disguise could produce—the whiskers, spectacles, and voice. Then I sent it to the firm, asking whether it described any of their travelling salesmen. I had already noted the typewriter's peculiarities, so I wrote to Windibank at his business address and invited him here. As I expected, he typed his reply, reproducing the same small but distinctive defects. The same post brought a letter from Westhouse & Marbank of Fenchurch Street confirming that the description matched their employee James Windibank in every detail. _Voilà tout_!”
“And what of Miss Sutherland?”

“She would not believe me if I told her. Perhaps you remember the old Persian saying: ‘There is danger for him who taketh the tiger cub, and danger also for whoso snatches a delusion from a woman.’ Hafiz contains as much wisdom as Horace, and as much understanding of the world.”
